### Chapter 21: The Equity Sleeve {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-21-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)

# The chapter's data, benchmark weights and sleeve constructor, repeated so that
# this fragment runs on its own.
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
eq <- sim_assets[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity", ]
A  <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly[sim_asset_returns_monthly$asset %in% eq$asset_id, ],
                date, asset, return)[, eq$asset_id]
region  <- setNames(eq$region, eq$asset_id)
regions <- c("US", "EU", "UK", "CH", "JP")
d <- zoo::index(A); X <- zoo::coredata(A)
stopifnot(identical(d, zoo::index(R)), !anyNA(A))

cap_w <- sim_marketcap_weekly[sim_marketcap_weekly$asset %in% eq$asset_id, ] |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = asset, values_from = market_cap) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
wk1 <- min(sim_asset_returns_weekly$date)
Cap <- as.matrix(cap_w[findInterval(c(wk1 - 1, d[-length(d)]), cap_w$date), eq$asset_id])
stopifnot(!anyNA(Cap), identical(colnames(Cap), colnames(X)))
bench_w <- function(t, j) Cap[t, j] / sum(Cap[t, j])

shrunk <- function(X) {
  S <- corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE)
  matrix(as.numeric(S), ncol(X), ncol(X), dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
}
te_of <- function(w, b, S) sqrt(12 * as.numeric(t(w - b) %*% S %*% (w - b)))
sleeve_family <- function(S, b, cap) {
  n <- length(b); Sb <- as.numeric(S %*% b)
  Amat <- cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n), -diag(n)); bvec <- c(1, rep(0, n), -cap)
  function(theta) {
    w <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, 2 * theta * Sb, Amat, bvec, meq = 1)$solution
    w <- pmax(w, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), names(b))
  }
}
select_sleeve <- function(S, b, tau, cap = pmax(0.10, b)) {
  f <- sleeve_family(S, b, cap); w0 <- f(0)
  if (te_of(w0, b, S) <= tau) return(w0)
  theta <- stats::uniroot(function(th) te_of(f(th), b, S) - tau, c(0, 1), tol = 1e-9)$root
  f(theta)
}
nw <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]; m <- stats::lm(x ~ 1)
  c(mean = 12 * mean(x), t = unname(stats::coef(m)) /
      sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)[1, 1]), months = length(x))
}
W <- 120L; oos <- seq.int(W + 1L, nrow(X))
us <- names(region)[region == "US"]
bench_us <- as.numeric(R[oos, "US_equity"])
rate <- pm_costs_default()[["equity"]]
```

#### Exercise 1

```{r}
#| label: sol-21-ex1
taus <- c(0.02, 0.04, 0.08)
ex1 <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(taus, function(tau) {
  Wm <- t(vapply(oos, function(t)
    select_sleeve(shrunk(X[(t - W):(t - 1L), us]), bench_w(t, us), tau), numeric(length(us))))
  r <- rowSums(Wm * X[oos, us]); a <- r - bench_us
  tibble::tibble(budget = tau, realized_te = stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12),
                 ir = mean(a) / stats::sd(a) * sqrt(12), vol = stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12),
                 eff_names = mean(1 / rowSums(Wm^2)))
}))
ex1 |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(budget, realized_te, vol), ~ sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * .x)),
                     ir = sprintf("%+.2f", ir), eff_names = sprintf("%.1f", eff_names)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrr", col.names = c("budget", "realized TE", "IR", "volatility", "effective names"))
```

The realized tracking error is not the budget. At two percent it comes out
`r if (ex1$realized_te[1] > taus[1]) "above" else "below"` the budget, at
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * ex1$realized_te[1])`, and at eight percent
`r if (ex1$realized_te[3] > taus[3]) "above" else "below"` it, at
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * ex1$realized_te[3])`. The budget is spent on the
*estimated* covariance of the trailing window, and the realized active return
is scored on months that matrix never saw, so the ex-post figure carries the
estimation error of @sec-08-estimation-error-theory in both directions;
the benchmark's weights also move between re-estimations. A larger budget buys
more of the distance to the minimum-variance portfolio, which is the lower
volatility in the fourth column, and the information ratio stays within a
standard error of zero at every budget, as the chapter found at four percent.

#### Exercise 2

```{r}
#| label: sol-21-ex2
mom6 <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(X), ncol(X), dimnames = dimnames(X))
for (t in 7:nrow(X)) mom6[t, ] <- apply(1 + X[(t - 6):(t - 2), ], 2, prod) - 1
wml <- function(signal, groups) vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(t) {
  if (anyNA(signal[t, ])) return(NA_real_)
  mean(vapply(regions, function(g) {
    j <- names(region)[region == g]; q <- dplyr::ntile(signal[t, j], groups)
    mean(X[t, j][q == groups]) - mean(X[t, j][q == 1])
  }, numeric(1)))
}, numeric(1))
rbind(`6-1, quintiles` = nw(wml(mom6, 5)), `6-1, terciles` = nw(wml(mom6, 3)))
```

Neither the shorter formation window nor the finer sort produces a momentum
spread distinguishable from zero: the quintile version earns
`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * nw(wml(mom6, 5))[["mean"]])` points a year at
$t = `r sprintf("%.2f", nw(wml(mom6, 5))[["t"]])`$. Had it appeared, it would
have to come from the common factors rather than from the names, because each
instrument's idiosyncratic draw is independent across periods; a factor-driven
momentum would show up as regional or sectoral return persistence, which is a
different object from the cross-sectional effect of @jegadeesh1993 and would
be visible in the class series of @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation
before it was visible here.

#### Exercise 3

```{r}
#| label: sol-21-ex3
Xus <- X[oos, us]; n <- length(us)
path_ew <- function(every) {                      # rebalance to 1/N every `every` months
  w <- rep(1 / n, n); out <- matrix(NA_real_, length(oos), 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("gross", "turnover", "cost")))
  for (i in seq_along(oos)) {
    target <- if ((i - 1L) %% every == 0L) rep(1 / n, n) else w
    trade <- sum(abs(target - w)); r <- sum(target * Xus[i, ])
    out[i, ] <- c(r, trade / 2, rate * trade)
    w <- target * (1 + Xus[i, ]) / (1 + r)
  }
  out
}
sharpe <- function(r) (prod(1 + r)^(12 / length(r)) - prod(1 + rf[oos])^(12 / length(r))) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
ex3 <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c(monthly = 1L, annual = 12L), function(k) {
  p <- path_ew(k)
  tibble::tibble(turnover = mean(p[, "turnover"]) * 12, gross = 12 * mean(p[, "gross"]),
                 sharpe_gross = sharpe(p[, "gross"]), sharpe_net = sharpe(p[, "gross"] - p[, "cost"]))
}), .id = "rebalanced")
ex3
```

Rebalancing annually cuts turnover from
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * ex3$turnover[ex3$rebalanced == "monthly"])` to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * ex3$turnover[ex3$rebalanced == "annual"])` a year
and changes the net Sharpe ratio by
`r sprintf("%+.3f", ex3$sharpe_net[ex3$rebalanced == "annual"] - ex3$sharpe_net[ex3$rebalanced == "monthly"])`.
In the decomposition of @plyakha2021 the annual portfolio keeps the size tilt,
since its average weights are still far closer to $1/N$ than to
capitalization, and gives up most of the contrarian trading; the gross return
gap between the two rows,
`r sprintf("%+.2f", 100 * (ex3$gross[ex3$rebalanced == "monthly"] - ex3$gross[ex3$rebalanced == "annual"]))`
points a year, is therefore an estimate of what the rebalancing itself
contributes, and the rest of the equal-weight premium of @tbl-21-ew-cw is the
tilt.

#### Exercise 4

```{r}
#| label: sol-21-ex4
r_ew <- rowMeans(Xus) - rf[oos]; r_b <- bench_us - rf[oos]
fit  <- stats::lm(r_ew ~ r_b)
alpha <- 12 * stats::coef(fit)[[1]]; beta <- stats::coef(fit)[[2]]
sig_e <- stats::sd(stats::residuals(fit)) * sqrt(12)
mu_b  <- 12 * mean(r_b); sig_b <- stats::sd(r_b) * sqrt(12)
w0    <- (alpha / sig_e^2) / (mu_b / sig_b^2)       # Treynor and Black: active against passive
w_tb  <- w0 / (1 + (1 - beta) * w0)                  # adjusted for the sleeve's beta
round(c(alpha = alpha, beta = beta, appraisal = alpha / sig_e, w_star = w_tb,
        sharpe_passive = mu_b / sig_b,
        sharpe_combined = sqrt((mu_b / sig_b)^2 + (alpha / sig_e)^2)), 4)
```

The equally weighted sleeve has an appraisal ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", alpha / sig_e)` against the United States benchmark, and
@eq-21-treynor-black would put `r sprintf("%.2f", w_tb)` units of the equity
money into it for every unit allocated, that is, all of it and a short
position in the index besides. The comparison with the
policy's budget is not one of like with like: $\omega$ in the chapter is the
share of the *whole* portfolio in equities, set by the tangency across sleeves,
while $\omega^{*}$ here is the share of the *equity* money in the active sleeve
rather than the passive one, and the two multiply rather than compete. What the
comparison does say is that the appraisal ratio is an in-sample estimate with
the standard error of @eq-24-se attached, so a weight computed from it inherits
the error-maximizing behavior of @sec-09-mean-variance-application; the
combined Sharpe ratio in the last line is the ceiling, not a forecast.
